metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Felker v. Turpin

Opinion filed: 1996-06-28

Docket No.: 95-8836

Citations:
• 135 L. Ed. 2d 827
• 116 S. Ct. 2333
• 518 U.S. 651
• 1996 U.S. LEXIS 4264

Case holding summaries:
• holding that the added restrictions on second habeas petitions are "well within the compass of this evolutionary process" and do not amount to a suspension of the writ
• provision barring a writ of certiorari for review of grant or denial of certain habeas petitions did not unconstitutionally infringe on Supreme Court's constitutional authority because nothing in AEDPA impaired the Court's original jurisdiction to issue a writ of habeas corpus
• discussing the “screening function” that courts must perform under the AEDPA
• noting that repeals by implication are not favored
• "[A]uthority to grant habeas relief to state prisoners is limited by § 2254, which specifies the conditions under which such relief may be granted to `a person in custody pursuant to the judgment of a State court.'" (citation omitted)
• “[W]e assume, for purposes of decision here, that the Suspension Clause . . . refers to the writ as it exists today, rather than as it existed in 1789.”
• AEDPA's restrictions on successive petitions "do not amount to a `suspension' of the writ"
• noting that the writ originally only extended to prisoners in federal custody who were not “detained in prison by virtue of the judgment of a court” (citation and internal quotation marks omitted)
• “The class of judicial actions reviewable by the writ [as known to the Framers] was more restricted as well.”
• discussing history of the writ
• implied repeals of habeas jurisdiction are disfavored
• noting that AEDPA’s restric- tions on second or successive petitions "are well within the compass" of the evolution of the abuse of the writ doctrine
• "The new restrictions on successive petitions constitute a modified res judicata rule, a restraint on what is called in habeas corpus practice 'abuse of the writ.' "
• expressly leaving open the question whether and to what extent the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA) applies to original petitions
• “[A]uthority to grant habeas relief to state prisoners is limited by § 2254, which specifies the conditions under which such relief may be granted to ‘a person in custody pursuant to the judgment of a State court.’”
• AEDPA's restrictions on "second or successive" petitions constitute "a restraint on what is called in habeas corpus practice 'abuse of the writ'"
• declining to find jurisdictional repeal by implication
• AEDPA restrictions on second habeas petitions are within compass of evolving abuse-of-the-writ principles and do not amount to unconstitutional suspension of writ
• the added restrictions which AEDPA places on second and successive petitions fall well within Congress' authority
• AEDPA’s restrictions on successive petitions “do not amount to a ‘suspension’ of the writ”
• declining to find jurisdictional repeal by implication
• acknowledging that AEDPA “work[ed] substantial changes” to the ability of a federal tribunal to entertain a habeas petition
• “[J]udgments about the proper scope of the writ are normally for Congress to make.” (internal quotations omitted)
• holding that AEDPA does not amount to a suspension of the writ contrary to Article I, §9
• holding § 2244(b)(1)’s “restrictions . . . do not amount to a ‘suspension’ of the writ contrary to [the Suspension Clause]”
• acknowledging that AEDPA “work[ed] substantial changes” to federal habeas law
• “[J]udgments about the proper scope of the writ are normally for Congress to make.”
• “[J]udgments about the proper scope of the writ are normally for Congress to make.”
• “Title I of the Act has changed the standards governing our consideration of habeas petitions by imposing new requirements for the granting of relief to state prisoners.”
• holding that the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court to entertain petitions for a writ of habeas corpus remains unaffected by the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act
• reviewing history of federal habeas corpus, including fact that statutes originally providing such authority were "direct ancestors" of provisions of § 2241
• explaining that AEDPA is “well within the compass of this evolutionary process”
• “[J]udgments about the proper scope of the writ are normally for Congress to make.”
• AEDPA’s restrictions on successive petitions “do not amount to a ‘suspension’ of the writ”
• holding that under the "clear statement" rule, § 2241 jurisdiction cannot be repealed by implication
• Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act (AEDPA)
• suggesting that courts Attorney General.”
• considering limitations on successive petitions
• applying different section of the AEDPA to pending case
• declining to conclude that Title I of AEDPA repealed habeas jurisdiction because it did not explicitly mention habeas corpus
• so holding with respect to the gatekeeping provisions applicable to successive § 2254 petitions
• AEDPA’s restrictions on successive petitions “do not amount to a ‘suspension’ of the writ”
• discussing AEDPA's "modified res judicata rule" under § 2244
• “[T]he Act . . . does not deprive this Court of jurisdiction to entertain original habeas petitions.”
• noting “judgments about the proper scope of the writ are normally for Congress to make” (quotation omitted)
• holding that successive-petition restrictions in 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b) do not violate the Suspension Clause
• quotation 22 Case: 18-30684 Document: 00515608112 Page: 23 Date Filed: 10/20/2020 No. 18-30684 omitted
• "the new restrictions on successive petitions constitute a modified res judicata rule, a restraint on what is called in habeas corpus practice 'abuse of the writ' "
• “[J]udgments about the proper scope of the writ are ‘normally for Congress to make.’”
